ch08 - Invitation to Initiation.md
chapters.relation: A short introduction that opens with the 'Hardhome' scene where Stannis tells Sam Tarly to 'keep reading' after learning from an old manuscript that dragonglass kills White Walkers, arguing that knowledge is itself a weapon in Westeros. Chaillan promises that the volume's philosophers ('Maester Kant on the King's Road,' 'Lord Machiavelli' in the Red Keep, Kierkegaard on Stannis) will initiate fans into the show's philosophical depth, from whether it is immoral to watch its violence to whether the Red Wedding can be justified.

chapters.file: ch09 - xi.md
ch10 - I. Life Is Not a Song.md
ch11 - 1. Arya Stark as a Rough Hero.md
chapters.relation: Dadlez asks whether Game of Thrones is morally defective for making audiences root for Arya Stark, a child murderer whose victims run from the insurance seller in Braavos to Walder Frey and his sons baked into a pie. Working through Hume's 'rough heroes' worry from 'Of the Standard of Taste' against Anne Eaton's 'robust immoralism' and the halo effect, she argues Martin's text never endorses Arya's killings but shows their cost to her - her suppression of doubt before the soup-shop assassination, her nightmare repetition of the names on her kill list, her reclaiming of 'Arya Stark of Winterfell' - so our investment is empathetic concern rather than corrupting approval, and the story is not ethically flawed.

chapters.file: ch12 - 2. Ned Stark One Man in Ten Thousand.md
chapters.relation: Kirby reads Ned Stark's arc through Aristotle's Poetics: his excessive honor is a hamartia ('too much of a good thing'), his acceptance of Robert's summons and refusal of Renly's help and Littlefinger's plan are the peripeteia, and the fan mourning after 'Baelor' is catharsis binding viewers into a community. With Martha Nussbaum's work on Greek tragedy he then argues the series' deepest lesson is tragic conflict - Agamemnon sacrificing Iphigenia mirrored by Stannis and Shireen, and Maester Aemon's 'love is the death of duty' warning to Jon - where no hierarchy of values dissolves the moral residue, so we must suffer into learning instead of trusting philosophical prioritization.

chapters.file: ch13 - 3. There’s Only One God and His Name Is Death.md
chapters.relation: McKeever observes that central characters rarely die suddenly and unexpectedly in art even though such deaths define our emotional lives, and argues this is a 'representational limit of art,' like Hollywood ugliness and costume-drama archaic speech. Using Plato's theory of art as a copy of a copy (a picture of Tyrion's chipped goblet imitating the Form of the goblet) and Aristotle's catharsis, he then argues Martin overcomes the limit through epic scale: with so many viewpoint characters, Ned can die at the end of season one and Joffrey mid-season-four because attention simply shifts, so making a work epic is the general cure for what art cannot represent.

chapters.file: ch14 - 4. Tyrion’s Humor.md
chapters.relation: Hietalahti reads Tyrion's wit - slapping Joffrey, his mock confession at the Eyrie, the dwarf-jester show at the Purple Wedding - through the classic theories of humor: Kant and Kierkegaard's incongruity, the Platonic-Hobbesian superiority laugh, and Freud's hidden hostility. Against those who see only a jester, he argues Tyrion's humor is social criticism grounded in what Erich Fromm calls affirmation of life: unlike the Joker, who laughs because nothing matters, Tyrion mocks hollow ritual, sham trials, and gods who want enemies burned because everyone matters, and having lost everything in A Dance with Dragons he still refuses the poisonous 'sweet death,' holding that life itself is worth living.

chapters.file: ch15 - II. There Are No Men Like Me, Only Me.md
ch16 - 5. Guilty of Being a Dwarf.md
chapters.relation: Engels runs Tyrion's arc through Sartre's existentialism: his facticity as a dwarf makes everyone from Catelyn to Tywin presume his guilt, while 'Never forget what you are, wear it like armor' states the Sartrean authenticity of owning facticity while freely choosing one's essence. Catelyn's dagger accusation, the comic confession at the Eyrie, the wildfire ship at Blackwater, and the trial outburst ('I am guilty of a far more monstrous crime: the crime of being a dwarf') show him choosing rather than being defined; the murders of Shae and Tywin dramatize the slide into bad faith - embracing the 'monster' essence others assigned - before his choice to join Daenerys resumes the burden of self-creation.

chapters.file: ch17 - 6. Jaime the Savior.md
chapters.relation: The Coxes defend Jaime's kingslaying with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Book III on voluntary, involuntary, and 'mixed' actions: like a storm-besieged crew jettisoning cargo, or the Blackfish's 'a knife to his throat is not a valid order,' Jaime faced a duress - kill Tywin on Aerys's order or let King's Landing burn - so his regicide was a mixed action that is praiseworthy as the least harmful option rather than blameworthy. They add Locke's right of revolution, where a ruler who makes his will rather than law the rule puts himself in a state of war with his people, to argue the Mad King's 'Burn them all' tyranny justified the killing, making the reviled Kingslayer the savior of the city.

chapters.file: ch18 - 7. Jon Snow, a Misshapen Christ Figure.md
chapters.relation: Rosa argues Westeros is a moral wasteland stripped of exemplars - heroes die, and vice spreads by imitation, as with Joffrey, Ramsay, and the Mountain - so Jon Snow functions as the series' Christ figure: the humble hidden king revealed in Bran's vision, the reformer uniting wildlings and Watch against death, killed by his brothers in 'Mother's Mercy' and risen in 'Home.' Using Aristotle's virtue ethics - Bran's archery lesson as the image of eudaimonia, hamartia as missing the mark, character formed by watching and imitating exemplars like Ned at the deserter's execution - the chapter claims the world is redeemable only through 'minority moral reform' embodied in a complete life, as with Jesus, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr.

chapters.file: ch19 - 8. Brienne and the Struggle for Recognition.md
chapters.relation: Giladi reads Brienne as a challenge to the Westerosi recognition order: winning the melee at Renly's camp and requesting the Kingsguard, she embodies knightly virtue in a society that deems it naturally male, and the crowd's bewildered, muted applause is a recognition injustice that withholds the social conditions of her self-confidence and authenticity. He analyzes Jaime's mockery in 'The Prince of Winterfell' - sexualizing her as 'boring as you are ugly' where he would never treat Barristan Selmy so - as stripping Brienne of her status as a conversational peer and equal rational enquirer, while the attempted gang-rape by Locke's men in 'Walk of Punishment' shows the violent backlash her struggle for recognition provokes.

chapters.file: ch20 - III. Power Is Power.md
ch21 - 9. Varys’s Riddle—Where Does Power Come From.md
chapters.relation: Iuliano uses Varys's riddle - king, priest, and rich man each bidding the same sellsword to kill the others - and 'power resides where men believe it resides' to stage a contest between John Austin's command theory of law (sovereign orders backed by force) and H.L.A. Hart's The Concept of Law, where authority rests on social acceptance. Cersei's 'power is power' scene with Littlefinger shows obedience that is mere coercion - Hart's gunman, being obliged rather than obligated - making the Lannisters gunmen writ large; the Hound's walkout on Joffrey exposes the illusion collapsing, and Plato's cave explains why Westerosi smallfolk prefer the comforting shadow to the truth that would free them.

chapters.file: ch22 - 10. How to Be Free.md
chapters.relation: O'Connell and Sirvent argue Seneca's Stoic freedom - release from fear of death and from every attachment - illuminates the two most enslaved groups in the story. The Unsullied's training strips them of possessions, names, lust, and fear, with Grey Worm's shame at fearing death for Missandei's sake showing exactly what attachment does to this freedom, while the Faceless Men's 'valar morghulis' mantra works like Seneca's recommended contemplation of death, letting Arya drink blindly from the cup at the House of Black and White. The chapter concludes that a fearlessness built by slaves and assassins really is a kind of freedom beyond their servitude, though Seneca would recoil at the brutal methods that produce it.

chapters.file: ch23 - 11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due.md
chapters.relation: Ewing argues money is the real determinant of the Iron Throne: Lannister gold made Cersei queen, Tyrell grain and taxation bought Margaery's crown, Baelish's financing decided the Battle of the Bastards, and the Iron Bank disciplines kings. Reading Westeros as a late-feudal economy through Marx - smallfolk whose work and taxes support lords who 'reap where they never sowed,' a hierarchy held by coercion and fear as the High Sparrow tells Olenna ('You are the few, we are the many'), and money dissolving feudal bonds into a 'money aristocracy' - he predicts the throne will go not to dragons or White Walkers but to the capitalist-financier figure of Petyr Baelish.

chapters.file: ch24 - 12. Margaery for Queen!.md
chapters.relation: Jones asks whether Margaery - who grooms Tommen, admits she was 'good at seeming good,' and may count as an abuser despite Westeros's norms - could still have been the best queen in the Seven Kingdoms. Against the prosecution's portrait of a cold egoist, he argues her charity to Flea Bottom's children shows a queen is good by what she does rather than why she did it, so selfish ambition welded to shrewdness can genuinely serve the common good. Comparing her with Ramsay (cruelty that provokes revolt) and Ned (benevolence without calculation that gets him killed), the chapter draws an implicitly Machiavellian conclusion - the people's best bet is hunger for power joined to the cunning to keep them onside - while doubting that cultural relativism can fully excuse her treatment of Tommen.

chapters.file: ch25 - 13. Bran, Hodor, and Disability in Westeros.md
chapters.relation: Pierce uses Westeros's many disabled characters - Bran's paralysis, Jaime's lost hand, Hodor, Aemon's blindness, Varys and Theon's castration - to test the medical and social models of disability and the 'mere difference' view, asking whether disability is merely unaccommodated impairment or intrinsically worse for the one who has it. With the left-handedness analogy and the distinction between local and global harm, he then pits Aristotle's natural teleology (legs are for walking and eyes for seeing, so their loss is a real local bad) against Lucretius's Epicurean anti-teleology (no purposes in nature, so no intrinsic lack), concluding that even if disabilities are locally bad, Bran, Hodor, and Varys can be globally flourishing and heroic.

chapters.file: ch26 - IV. The Things I Do for Love.md
ch27 - 14. The Gods Hate Incest.md
chapters.relation: Barkman defends the near-universal Westerosi condemnation of incest. Against Freud's Oedipal account - which Jaime and Cersei's childhood romance seems to fit - he deploys Edward Westermarck's aversion hypothesis, primate evidence, and the Taiwanese simpua-marriage studies to argue that co-raised siblings should feel natural sexual aversion, so the twins are either instinctually malformed or unconvincingly written, while cases like Black Walder and Littlefinger with Sansa fit the effect fine. He then grounds the taboo in Natural Law - deduced from 'do no harm,' care of the weak, and natural family roles, plus the harms of inbreeding and endogamy - and concludes that children of incest like Joffrey are abominations by choice, not by birth.

chapters.file: ch28 - 15. Joffrey on the Couch.md
chapters.relation: Wills asks why audiences so relish hating Joffrey and answers with Freud's Totem and Taboo: the incest taboo was instituted precisely because the desire persists in the unconscious, and Joffrey - the product of 'accumulative incest' with cousin-grandparents and sibling parents - embodies the broken taboo. Reading the furious fan reactions (his death 'wasn't horrible enough,' the meticulous lists of his worst acts) as projection and successful repression, the chapter argues that vilifying Joffrey channels our own repressed taboo-breaking urges, while Westeros's distanced past setting lets us dissociate from the savagery exactly as Freud's staging of primitive peoples did.

chapters.file: ch29 - 16. Hope for Bastards and Sand Snakes.md
chapters.relation: Desveaux argues the hidden organizing concept of Game of Thrones is filiation - the legal system that transmits family belonging, name, status, and destiny. Sigils and house colors (the blond Lannister children as visible evidence of incest), Ned's law-enforcing beheading of the deserter, and the nature-names of bastards - Snow in the North, Sand in Dorne - all display its force: Jon's authenticity and open-mindedness come from standing outside it, Ramsay's legitimization after the Red Wedding and the Sand Snakes' Dornish independence mark its exceptions, while whores and smallfolk beyond all filiation have no protection at all, a contrast the chapter uses to measure how far modern law has removed these penalties.

chapters.file: ch30 - 17. Sex, Consent, and Rape in Westeros.md
chapters.relation: Underwood distinguishes the legal consent of fifteenth-century-style Westeros - under the conjugal-debt doctrine neither Drogo nor Ramsay legally raped their wives, while every Cersei-Jaime union was treasonous regardless of desire - from the moral standard of consent developed from Alan Wertheimer's work. Applying his fraud and disregard cases, she argues Sansa's marriage obtained through Littlefinger's deception and Daenerys's coerced early nights with Drogo are immoral though legal, and proposes 'reciprocal subjectivity' as the criterion: Ramsay treats Sansa purely as an object, but the scene at Joffrey's body shows Jaime raping Cersei while still loving her as a subject, proving mutual recognition is necessary yet not sufficient for morally permissible sex.

chapters.file: ch31 - V. I Swear before the Old Gods and the New.md
ch32 - 18. Gods and Beetles.md
chapters.relation: Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies. Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'

chapters.file: ch33 - 19. Prophetic Foreknowledge in Game of Thrones.md
chapters.relation: Rennick argues that true prophecy threatens no one's freedom: a true prophecy merely reports the future the way a true history book reports the past - Jojen sees Jon among the wildlings because Jon chose as he chose, not the reverse - while fallible, misread prophecies (Melisandre mistaking Alys Karstark for Arya, the Stallion prophecy dying with Rhaego) constrain even less. Self-fulfilling prophecies like Azor Ahai actually demonstrate agency, since Stannis and Melisandre's belief in the prophecy brings the events about, and even infallible foreknowledge of a choice - 'you will watch season seven' - leaves open the alternate Westeros where you did otherwise, the standard reply to the God's-foreknowledge problem applied to green dreams and flames.

chapters.file: ch34 - 20. Cersei, Sansa, and the Problem of Evil.md
chapters.relation: McCrossin reads Cersei and Sansa's post-imprisonment rises in season six as opposite answers to the problem of evil, framed by Susan Neiman's claim that Enlightenment thought split between making evil intelligible and refusing to. Cersei, taught by Tywin that 'the gods have no mercy - that's why they're gods,' becomes Sade's cruel god of Juliette, doing whatever feels good as the gods do; Sansa, hardened by Ramsay and Littlefinger's betrayal into 'no one can protect anyone,' embodies the Kantian response that virtue and happiness come apart, so one governs only what can be controlled - character, family, justice - as she engineers the Battle of the Bastards and has Ramsay eaten by his dogs without mercy or vengeance.

chapters.file: ch35 - 21. Stannis—Knight of Faith or Tragic Hero.md
chapters.relation: Devlin asks whether Stannis, who burns Shireen to save his army, is Kierkegaard's knight of faith or merely a tragic hero. Stannis's duty-obsessed deontology - knighting Davos while cutting off his fingertips, striking 'beloved brother' from a letter as a lie - is Kantian, and the Shireen dilemma looks like Abraham's teleological suspension of the ethical; yet because Stannis always calculates and justifies ('Faith? In a real war, the side with the greater number wins nine times out of ten'), he never makes the leap on the strength of the absurd, and Davos ends up following Kant's own verdict on Abraham: 'If he commands you to burn children, your lord is evil.' He is therefore a tragic hero in the line of Agamemnon and Jephthah, rationally comprehensible and fittingly undone by Brienne's 'do your duty.'

chapters.file: ch36 - 22. The Many-Faced God and Indian Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Van Eyghen maps the Faceless Men onto Indian philosophy: their one God of many faces parallels Vedanta's Brahman in personal form as Ishvara, and Arya's training to become 'no one' parallels shedding the ego toward identity with Brahman - with Jaqen as guru and the stick-beating ritual as an example of identity fusion in Harvey Whitehouse's cognitive science of religion. But the Faceless Men may go further than Vedanta toward Buddhism, since they worship a god with no face of his own and aim at no-self rather than union, while Arya's pragmatic adoption of the shellfish-merchant disguise echoes the Bhagavad Gita's Krishna: perform your duty without attachment to any self.

chapters.file: ch37 - VI. Knowledge Is Power.md
ch38 - 23. How Can We Know Anything in a World of Magic and Miracles.md
chapters.relation: Baldwin asks whether Westerosi characters can know anything inductive in a world without lawlike nature: seasons of unpredictable length, wargs in animal minds, Faceless Men changing faces, and resurrections by Thoros, Melisandre, and Qyburn. After laying out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge (those who saw the pyre are justified in believing Dany is the mother of dragons; those relying on rumor are not), he runs Hume's problem of induction - we never perceive causal connection, so no jar of wildfire must explode - against Reid's common-sense reply that reason and induction stand or fall together, concluding that Westeros gives its people special reasons for skepticism while we, lacking evidence of magical irregularity, are rational to trust everyday inductive belief.

chapters.file: ch39 - 24. Samwell Tarly’s Renaissance.md
chapters.relation: Alves reads Westeros as a technologically stagnant society where knowledge is hoarded by monopolies - the Maesters' Citadel chain links and the Alchemists' wildfire secret - and asks what Samwell Tarly's library discoveries at Castle Black plus his battlefield experience with dragonglass against the White Walkers add up to. Arguing that empiricism - observation and experiment against the dubious authority of old texts, the mix that birthed modern science out of alchemy and astrology (with Mircea Eliade and even Newton as border cases) - is exactly what Sam practices, the chapter suggests he is igniting a Westerosi renaissance of lost Valyrian-age knowledge, while the Doom of Valyria warns, like Prometheus and Babel, against knowing too much.

chapters.file: ch40 - 25. Should Catelyn Have Trusted Brienne.md
chapters.relation: McNabb and Andrews ask whether Catelyn was warranted in trusting Brienne as her sworn sword after Brienne failed to save Renly, and test two theories of warrant. On accessibilist coherentism, Catelyn's accessible evidence - Brienne's prowess, her devastation at Renly's death, 'Renly's death was no fault of yours' - fits her web of beliefs like a new strand in a spider's web; on Plantinga-style proper functionalism, illustrated by the accident-created Labman replica and the Lord of Light randomizing a design plan, Catelyn's naturally formed belief that Brienne is trustworthy is warranted if her faculties are properly functioning, truth-aimed, and well designed - which Brienne's record through rescuing Sansa vindicates.

chapters.file: ch41 - VII. You Think I Would Trade My Honor.md
ch42 - 26. Horrifying Violence, Gratuitous Sex, and the Truth.md
chapters.relation: Silverman concedes Game of Thrones can be watched viciously - sadistically relishing Theon's flaying or using it as soft pornography - but denies the show is inherently immoral. From Plato's Republic he takes the test of whether a narrative serves or obscures reality (Socrates was executed partly on the slander of Aristophanes' Clouds) and argues the show is honest where epics lie: war is ugly and kills innocents, measured against the Augustinian just-war criteria that even the Brotherhood Without Banners decays past; humans really are as sexually preoccupied as Plato's appetitive soul, Freud's id, or Augustine's original sin; and honor without practical wisdom - Ned versus Tyrion on Aristotle's ideal - is a recipe for ruin.

chapters.file: ch43 - 27. Was the Red Wedding Massacre a Good Thing.md
chapters.relation: Van der Deijl takes Tywin's line to Tyrion - 'explain to me why it is more noble to kill ten thousand men in battle than a dozen at dinner' - as a serious consequentialist challenge about the Red Wedding. Working through utilitarianism, prioritarianism, and dirty-hands cases like Hiroshima and shooting down a hijacked plane, he concedes the massacre could have been justified had breaking Guest Right and killing 3,500 brought peace at minimal cost; but the consequences fail - Joffrey and Roose Bolton keep power, the institution of guest right erodes, and Tywin's real motive was family power rather than the greater good - so the massacre fails even the consequentialist test, and Tywin is a power-hungry conspirator, not Machiavelli's prince.

chapters.file: ch44 - 28. Severed Heads, Dirty Hands.md
chapters.relation: Ivanković and Božac argue that ruling Westeros necessarily means dirtying one's hands, staging the paradox through Varys's counsel to Ned and Jaime's 'finest act.' Hobbes supplies the baseline that anything preserving peace beats the war of all against all, Walzer permits dirty hands only to avert communal death (Daenerys swindling the Astapor slavers), and Kant's absolute refusal to lie - mirrored in Ned's honor - costs Ned his head and the realm a war. The chapter also indicts the reverse: Aemon's refusal of the throne and other too-clean refusals of responsibility are moral failures, Jon's killing of Qhorin Halfhand shows dirty hands are not just for kings, and rulers must resist the downward spiral while keeping, as Dany does, a gentle heart for the true goal.

chapters.file: ch45 - 29. The Best of Friends.md
chapters.relation: Geyer sorts Game of Thrones friendships by Aristotle's three kinds in the Nicomachean Ethics. Robert and Ned's bond, formed in Jon Arryn's fosterage and shared war, is friendship of pleasure, which frays over Rhaegar's 'dragonspawn'; Tyrion and Bronn is friendship of utility, dissolving exactly as Aristotle predicts when Lollys's marriage pays better than a trial by combat in 'Mockingbird'; and Jon and Sam, each valuing the other's character for its own sake at the Wall, approach the only true friendship - the virtue friendship - supporting the claim that eudaimonia needs such relationships alongside external goods.

chapters.file: ch46 - 30. Trying to Do Good with Arya, Tyrion, and the Hound.md
chapters.relation: Thomas sets Aristotle's practical wisdom against Bentham's utility calculus and Kant's consequence-proof rules, then watches all three struggle in season six. Arya's merciful refusal to poison Lady Crane backfires when the Waif kills her more painfully anyway; Tyrion's compromise with the Masters - phasing out slavery gradually, 'I trust their self-interest' - nearly loses Meereen when they attack by sea; and the resurrected Hound, after Brother Ray's massacre, concludes that 'lots of horrible shit in this world gets done for something larger than ourselves,' so being good in Westeros, as everywhere, means choosing without being able to know the consequences in advance.

chapters.file: ch47 - 31. Paying the Iron Price.md
chapters.relation: Hansberger reads Theon's return to the Iron Islands as an Aristotelian failure of virtue: excess lust toward Yara on the road, the 'small soul' of gold-bought jewelry where Balon demands iron-price honor, and the rashness rather than courage of trying to hold Winterfell with twenty men. But Balon's virtues are the vices of a piratical society that rewards reaving and rape, and through Charles Taylor's ethics of authenticity the chapter argues Theon's deeper failure is not knowing who he is - Stark or Greyjoy - so Ramsay's breaking of him into Reek completes a collapse of self that began at home; authenticity, it concludes, depends on virtue and social relations, which is why Theon can only begin to recover by choosing to serve Yara.

chapters.file: ch49 - References.md
ch50 - Lineages and Histories of the Great Maesters.md
ch51 - Index.md

holes.name: The Standard of Taste (Rough Heroes)
holes.what: Hume's essay 'Of the Standard of Taste' arguing that art is judged by refined sentiment and that morally 'rough heroes' we plainly discover to be blameable cannot properly engage our imagination.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire argument over whether Game of Thrones is morally flawed for making the child-killer Arya lovable runs on Hume's standard of taste versus Anne Eaton's 'robust immoralism' and halo effect.

holes.name: Tragic Conflict (the fragility of goodness)
holes.what: Nussbaum's idea, drawn from Greek tragedy, that luck can force a person to choose between two equally valid moral claims so that every option involves real loss and moral residue.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia, Stannis's parallel sacrifice of Shireen, and Aemon's honor-versus-love advice to Jon to argue that no prioritization of values can dissolve genuine tragic conflicts.

holes.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of how tragedy represents misfortune so audiences vent or purge emotions like pity and fear.
holes.why: Chapter 13 builds its account of why art rarely depicts sudden death, and how Game of Thrones represents life's fragility, on the Platonic-Aristotelian mimesis-and-catharsis framework.

holes.name: Erich Fromm
holes.what: Humanistic psychoanalyst who located humanity's essence in its existential contradictions and held that the good life is 'affirmation of life' - love, growth, and principled disobedience to hollow authority.
holes.why: Chapter 14 frames Tyrion's humor and refusal to submit as Frommian life-affirmation against empty court ritual, citing Fromm by name as the chapter's central positive framework.

holes.name: Voluntary, Involuntary and Mixed Actions
holes.what: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Book III distinction, used to judge blameworthiness: acts done under compulsion or duress are 'mixed' and can be pardonable or even praiseworthy when they choose the lesser evil for a noble end.
holes.why: Chapter 17's whole defense of Jaime's kingslaying rests on treating the regicide ordered under Aerys's duress as an Aristotelian mixed action rather than a voluntary crime.

holes.name: John Austin
holes.what: Nineteenth-century legal philosopher whose command theory defines law as the sovereign's command backed by the threat of force, the first scientific (positivist) theory of law.
holes.why: Chapter 21 uses Austin's command theory to give voice to Cersei's 'Power is power' and the three great men of Varys's riddle, before dismantling it.

holes.name: H.L.A. Hart
holes.what: Legal philosopher whose The Concept of Law replaced Austin's command theory, holding that law's authority rests on social acceptance of a rule of recognition rather than on coercive force.
holes.why: Chapter 21 argues through Hart's gunman/sovereign and obliged/obligated distinctions that the Lannisters are 'gunmen writ large' whose power, as Varys says, is only a trick, a shadow on the wall.

holes.name: The Westermarck Effect
holes.what: Edward Westermarck's hypothesis that living in close childhood intimacy produces a natural sexual aversion, explaining the incest taboo as an evolved instinct rather than repressed desire.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues Jaime and Cersei's relationship is written against Westermarck's evidence (primate studies, simpua marriages) and contrasts his natural-aversion account with Freud's Oedipal theory.

holes.name: Filiation (legal parentage and legitimacy)
holes.what: The legal system determining who belongs to which family, conferring name, status, inheritance, and destiny on children and punishing those outside it.
holes.why: Chapter 29 argues the whole Game of Thrones social order runs on filiation - bastard names like Snow and Sand, Ramsay's legitimization, the Sand Snakes' freedom, and the defenselessness of the unfiliated all derive from it.

holes.name: Moral vs Legal Consent
holes.what: Alan Wertheimer's distinction between sex that violates the law and sex that violates dignity or agency while remaining legal, including sex obtained by fraud or by disregard of the partner's status as a consenting subject.
holes.why: Chapter 30 uses it to show that Drogo legally never raped Daenerys yet morally raped her, and to sort the Sansa-Ramsay and Cersei-Jaime cases into legal, moral, and reciprocal-subjectivity failures.

holes.name: Susan Neiman
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher whose Evil in Modern Thought traces the problem of evil from its theological form to a secular one about virtue and happiness diverging, split between making evil intelligible and refusing to.
holes.why: Chapter 34 builds its whole contrast between Cersei's Sadean and Sansa's Kantian responses to suffering on Neiman's historical account of the problem of evil.

holes.name: Empiricism (knowledge from observation and experiment)
holes.what: The view that sensory observation and practical experiment are the best sources of knowledge, contrasted with deference to textual authority, tradition, or occult secrecy.
holes.why: Chapter 39 argues Samwell Tarly's combination of field experience with dragonglass and rediscovered library knowledge makes him the empiricist who can start a Westerosi renaissance against the Maesters' monopoly.

holes.name: Proper Functionalism (warrant)
holes.what: Plantinga's externalist theory of warrant: a belief is warranted when produced by truth-aimed cognitive faculties functioning properly in the environment for which they were designed.
holes.why: Chapter 40 defends Catelyn's trust in Brienne through proper functionalism, using the Labman replica and the Lord of Light's randomized design plan as its test cases.

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who defends authenticity - being true to oneself - as a genuine ethical ideal forged in dialogue and relationships with others, despite its self-indulgent misuses.
holes.why: Chapter 47 explains Theon's collapse into Reek through Taylor's Ethics of Authenticity, arguing that identity is formed in relationships and that authenticity depends on virtue.
